utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. [French on English channel]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm listening to French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're listening to French. You should be on channel 4. We'll get that adjusted for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm now back in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That sounds familiar, perhaps. Channel 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I now work for the other side. There was one thing I wanted to raise, if I may, and that is that yesterday the Prosecution asked me some questions about dates, and I've just did a bit of checking last night, and so if it helps I can set out precisely the date framework and a couple -- a few bits more information. As I understand it, NATO struck on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 1999, at 8 p.m. Belgrade time. The next morning, on Thursday, the 25th of March, according to an Albanian witness, from uncle Mehmet Abduli. He told me - and others did as well - but he told me specifically his information was good, I thought. But they arrived -- this convoy arrived at 3.40 a.m. very early in the morning. Tanks, half-tracks, and he said 15 buses, with Serb registrations on the buses from Nis and Leskovac. One had "Express Nis" written on it. He reckoned there were 50 men to each bus, so that's 750 men on the buses, and then the men's on the tanks and the half-tracks. He said that there were volunteers with blue police fatigues with white militia armbands and all armed. Now, on their arrival the Albanians in the village ran to the hills, and that is, if you understand the geography, you have the mountains of Albania, and then you have the river Drina, I'm going east as it were, and then you have the main road and the village, and then further east there is a bluff, wooded, and that's where the majority of the villagers ran. They were -- the Serbs fired shells at them, some kind of artillery, and they stayed out there the night. The next morning, the morning of Friday, the 26th of March, they realised that they had been surrounded. Some of the Serb forces had gone on the other side of them, and so the villagers surrendered. Then they all came back to the village of Mala Krusa. Then there was the selection. It was at this selection that Granny Batusha recognised Dimitri Nikolic. So when I said the name Dimitri Nikolic, that's where she in particular places him, and she called out Dimitri, and he looked away. Mehmet Abduli, himself, he recognised, he says, others, but I don't want to -- well, the names I've got are the names I've got. In terms of the numbers, it's hard to put a precise number on, but I believe my best estimate was 109 men in the hay barn of whom six survived. That number may be wrong, but the order magnitude is right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The oldest was a man called Bali Avdyli who was 72, the youngest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll see the Defence. THE COURT REPORTER: Sorry, can you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll see the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll do this. The oldest was Bali Avdyli, 72; the youngest was Xhelal Shehu, 13. Do you want me to spell those?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I see that the witness is reading from a little notebook. He didn't do that yesterday; he is doing that today. I would ask him to have the witness just explain what notebook he's using today, why he didn't use it yesterday, and what this is all about today, before he continues with his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I couldn't see the notebook from here, Mr. Djordjevic. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a simple notebook. Essentially I wrote a series of articles associated with the film for my newspaper. I re-read the articles, and I've got the dates, which I've written down in this notebook. This is simply a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are these notes you made last night, is what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But also, yesterday I didn't have in front of me my statement. Simply, and I'm expanding a little bit, but I want to be able to tell you the dates of the programme. That was the precise question that I couldn't remember. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think what you've done so far is to enable us to understand more precisely the time of some of the events you spoke of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yesterday from your own understanding overnight. It would be better now if you left off what you were doing and put away your notebook, and Mr. Djordjevic can proceed with his questions, and if there's anything more needs to be followed up in your re-examination, Ms. Kravetz will be able to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure thing. I'll put it away. It's just I've got the precise dates of when I entered Kosovo, when I first went to Little Krusa, and the dates of the two films.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. If you want any of those, Mr. Djordjevic, you can ask for them, or else Ms. Kravetz may in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think that this intervention will do, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I'm Dragoljub Djordjevic, Defence counsel for the accused Vlastimir Djordjevic. I'm an attorney-at-law. Mr. Sweeney, I'm going to put a few questions to you now that primarily have to do with your testimony yesterday. Also, my questions relate to the statement that you gave on the 22nd of January, 23rd of January, and 24th of January, 2001, to an investigator of the OTP. Now I'm going to start my series of questions. I heard from you yesterday, like we all did, that you are an experienced journalist and that you've been doing that kind of work for almost 20 years. Over the past 10 or 12 years, as you've said, you've been involved in investigative journalism. I would kindly ask you to explain this genre of journalism in the briefest possible terms. What is this investigative journalism, and what do you mean when you say that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good question. All journalism is, in some sense, investigative because what we're trying to do is tell -- tell people things they perhaps don't already know or they don't appreciate the significance of. What I've tried to do is to -- is to tell stories which are worth telling, which aren't invading people's privacy, doing stories about the Royal Family. I would hate that; I don't like that. The stories -- I prefer to do stories that powerful people don't want told, and they're stories that must be well-evidenced. So, in a sense, the most important thing is you've got good evidence something bad that's going on and you put it out, and you put it out fairly and squarely. And there are often bits which don't make sense or don't initially make sense or are in some ways against the -- against the flow. And it's very important to report those, too, as well. So that is -- my essential description of what I do is telling stories powerful people don't want told.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This kind of reporting, does it mean that there should be objectivity involved and should the nature of your work be documentary?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we're speaking specifically about the report that you compiled for channel 4 and for your newspaper - I believe that you said that you were writing for The Observer at the time - did you make assessments that were lopsided because you did not obtain enough information beforehand?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not perfect; I'm only human. But you'd have to give me slightly more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the then-Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? What were its bordering states, especially the Autonomous Province of Kosovo? If you give me an answer to this effect, could you also refer to the cardinal points - north, south, east, west? Who are the neighbours on north, south, east, west?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I've been to Yugoslavia. I first went to Yugoslavia in March 1991 after Mr. Milosevic sent the tanks in against the students in Belgrade. As I understand it to the north -- well, of former Yugoslavia, to the north-west you've got Italy; above it you've got Austria; around the side you've got Hungary and Romania; and down the bottom, next to Macedonia, you've have Greece and Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about Kosovo, as an autonomous province? What states does it border? I am not referring to Serbia and Montenegro at that time because they later established a country that was called the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which was in fact a federation of two states, the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro. Within the Republic of Serbia, we will agree that there were two autonomous provinces: One is Vojvodina and the other one is Kosovo and Metohija. So what were the border states on the south of Kosovo and also what about the border on the west? Or to be more specific, on the south-west? And what about the east?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking -- well, obviously I've just said Albania, and Greece, then you -- I don't think it touches Bulgaria. Macedonia was part of the former Yugoslavia. I'm not entirely clear what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, the Federal Republic. I'll tell you what I'm getting at, and I will ask you now specifically whether you will agree with me that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is to say, not the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, at the time of the conflict in 1999, we have a country that is called the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, whereas the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had not been in existence for quite a while by then. Will we agree that Kosovo or, rather, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the south borders the Republic of Macedonia, which is called the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's because of the dispute with Greece.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just slow down your question. It's not even a question but parts of it are questions. But it's very long, and it's becoming extremely difficult for those trying to do so to keep up with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good point, Your Honour. Good point. I shall abide by that in the future. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So, on the south it borders the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. On the south-west there's the Republic of Albania. And within that framework, on the north there is the so-called Serbia proper, and on the west, the present-day Republic of Montenegro, which is now an independent state but at that time was within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Can we agree on those facts?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. My next question: You mention figures in your statements ranging between 700.000 and 800.000 Kosovo Albanians who fled to Albania. Can we agree that that is what you had said?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't want to -- I'm a human being. I didn't count every single Kosovo Albanian who left Kosovo after the NATO strike. So essentially what we were doing was relying upon estimates that the international -- various international bodies, like the Red Cross, and various UN bodies were giving out. And that was the rough -- those rough numbers which are reported at the time. I believe they were accurate at the time. If there are new numbers, which I would imagine would be smaller numbers, that wouldn't surprise me. And I would make this distinction in my evidence to this Court. There are things that I heard about and reported, both on the film and in my newspaper, and then there are things that I have seen with my own eyes. So, I would say with my own eyes I have seen the holes in the ground of the Batusha hay barn was, evidence of a massacre covered up. I would say as to the 800.000 refugees --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We'll deal with that later.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, but you appreciate the distinction between the two, between things which I'm reporting because I've heard them and things which I've seen with my own eyes?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As for these groups that you are referring to now, we're going to deal with that later, Mr. Sweeney. The objective of my cross-examination is to get to the truth, the truth that you have in your hands, of course, and with mistakes that are permissible. Well, you've been saying that you're a human being and I fully respect that, so perhaps there weren't any mistakes. But my next question now: Do you know that the Kosovo Albanians did not only flee to Albania but also to the then-Yugoslav Republic of Montenegro and to the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia and even to Serbia? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you agree with me that the figure that we discussed a few moments ago, and you say that the source are governmental and other international organisations, like the Red Cross, et cetera, when we look at this figure in reference to absolutely all the refugees who fled from Kosovo, are you referring to all of those who fled or only the Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my number was -- the number in the film, I believe, is it 800.000, and they are essentially Kosovo Albanians fleeing after the NATO strike and then the Serb military attack on the Kosovar population in the spring of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sweeney. However, when we're talking about objectivity and figures, part of my cross-examination is geared towards that, as you've realised by now. The first thing that we're looking at is your arrival in Kosovo with the NATO forces. So you or the reporter, I mean we -- I think it's your voice, but we haven't discussed that. It doesn't really matter because you said that it doesn't matter. You enter Kosovo where tens of thousands of Albanians were killed. You said that later on you familiarised yourself with the facts that the figure is between 3.000 and 5.000, according to the official sources. Can you tell me, is this not a sensationalist way of writing? If you say tens of thousands, that is at least 20.000 and that is ten times more than what the figure actually was. I assume that you and I will both agree that it is a shame if a single person loses his or her life, but isn't this a bit too much?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem is that you're speaking with the benefit of hindsight. At the time we didn't know for a fact. All we did know is that in the spring, in March 1999, hundreds of thousands of Albanians fled and they said their relatives had been massacred and killed and their homes had been destroyed. And we could see some of that evidence, and for myself I went to the highlands of Albania and saw tens of thousands of people pass me day in, day -- you would go away and come back and that would continue. But these numbers were -- they were accurate, not sensationalist, when I reported them at the time. The number of dead, it's very, very difficult to check on a massacre, how many people have you killed, if you're banned from the country, if the authorities don't allow reporters to go with the military. So what you're asking me to do is to be absolutely accurate as to the numbers of people who fled and were killed at a time when it was impossible to do so. And I don't think to do the impossible or to fail to achieve the impossible is -- I don't think it's fair to call that sensationalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sweeney. My next question: Do you know, this figure that you referred to, the official one, 3.000 to 5.000 people who lost their lives in Kosovo, does this figure pertain to Kosovo Albanians only, or does it pertain to all the ethnic communities that lived in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine it -- I would imagine it pertains to everybody. What's the date of that figure?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There are many sources. Not a single one is very precise, as you've said. The first estimates started in June 1999. Different international organisations, like the International Red Cross and Red Crescent, then other non-governmental organisations, and to this day some organisations are providing their estimates but no one has said so far that 5.000 citizens of Kosovo had lost their lives. Also, will you agree with me in reference to this figure that it is not a reference only to civilians but rather the total number of fatalities in Kosovo, regardless of whether they were members of the KLA or some other formation, not to go into ethnic affiliation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think to an extent we're agreeing with each other that there is a question here about the number of people who fled and who were killed in Kosovo. Now, all I can do as a reporter at the time, in the spring and the summer of 1999, is report the numbers. For example, I also covered September the 11th, 2001, and I remember there was a front page of the Daily Telegraph saying, 60.000 feared dead in Manhattan. And in reality the number turned out to be 3.000, far higher. The point is thousands of people were killed. So what I know to be a fact is that thousands of people were killed, the precise number I don't know. But obviously it's the nature of human beings is that the first number's in the shock of the moment, you don't understand quite how many has happened. But to go on to argue that because the numbers at first -- at first glance put out by the international organisations were far too high does not mean that people were not killed. People were killed. I saw the dead bodies, and I certainly have spoken to people who said that they'd never seen their loved ones again, for example, the Albanian Kosovars of Little Krusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since you've mentioned the 11th of September, I didn't really want to ask you about this, but did you write a book about Saddam Hussein?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that after September 11th, the basic strategy of the foreign policy primarily of the United States and of the entire international community, which I fully justify, was struggle against terrorism?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be. Some of that struggle, as you call it, may not have been wise or right. But do carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I do beg your pardon for this digression. Then a war ensued in the Middle East. I'm not going to refer to particular persons or states or the consequences of all of this that no one can really like. My next question, Mr. Sweeney, it has to do with what we've been discussing so far. After that, when you found out that it wasn't tens of thousands of citizens of Kosovo that got killed, did you publish this information, that the total number of fatalities was between 3.000 and 5.000, actually? Did you publish that in any media in 1999 onwards?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, the critical question is when did the world community know that the true figure was between 3.000 -- 3.000 and 5.000. So forgive me, but it seems that you're criticising me for not getting a figure, the date of which I don't know. So what was your date for that figure? When was that first figure enter the international arena?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not criticising you, Mr. Sweeney. I'm just putting questions to you and I'm expecting answers, because we are not allowed to debate matters with witnesses. We are just allowed to put questions. My next question now --

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't answer your question unless you tell me the basis on which you put the question. So if you don't tell me the date of that number, then I can't answer your question. Not because I don't want to; it's because you haven't given me enough information. So when you say the official number is 3.000 to 5.000, what date is it? Because my next point was that if it's after 1999, it's unfair for you to criticise me for a date which wasn't available at that time, in particular in the summer of 1999 when I was reporting on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not criticising you, but you said, Afterwards I found out that the number of casualties was between 3.000 and 5.000. So when did you find out? On what date?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as time has gone on, the number has gone down, but I haven't followed -- it's a perfectly good explanation. I haven't followed the story of the massacre in Kosovo in every detail for the rest of my reporting career. I was there at the time, I was conscious that thousands of people had been killed, and that was correct. Now, the nature of journalism, certainly if you're making TV films, documentary films, is you don't go back to the subject and say, That number, by the way, was wrong. I'm very happy to say that here now. So there's no question about it, because I'm not responsible for that number. All I am responsible for is the fair reporting. And the point is that when the international community, because NATO's military machine got into Kosovo, then the war crimes people and the forensic people could start counting bodies and taking statements from the Albanians. That was impossible when Mr. Milosevic's men were ruling Kosovo. So you cannot criticise me for any number I generated before the NATO got in and opened up Kosovo to the possibility of fair and honest information-gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, have you ever heard the term "collateral damage"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When was the first time you came across that particular term?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's obviously a phrase that's used in Hollywood films. I believe it first emerged in Vietnam. It's a ghastly lying phrase which tries to hide -- "collateral damage" it tries to dehumanise when armies make terrible mistakes and bomb civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We'll easily agree on that. You do remember Mr. Jamie Shea, the NATO spokesperson and his reports. He often used the term, as a matter of fact, "collateral damage," exactly as we quoted. Shall we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps have information to the effect how many civilians exactly were killed in Kosovo as a result of collateral damage which in -- was the consequence of NATO, the air raids, strikes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, do you have any information indicating how many civilians were killed as collateral damage as a result of the activities performed by the Serb military and police forces as they were trying to put down the unrest in Kosovo? Do you perhaps have that information?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid that question opens up a very, very bitter debate, because if you say that it was the number of civilians who were killed while the Serb forces were trying to put down unrest, I know of specific stories where Serbs murdered people, murdered civilians - this is in 1998 - and arrested, tortured, abused people. So the Albanians would say, the Kosovars would say, that this was no peace-keeping exercise. So we're not comparing like with like. It's a bitter dispute. I do know -- I would imagine -- I remember when NATO had forces bombed the Belgrade TV transmitter, and there was a number of journalists who were killed. I thought that was wrong, not just because I'm journalist, because I don't believe that knocking out other people's journalists is a good thing to do. I have often said the thing of ambulance workers as well, obviously journalists aren't anything near as useful as people who drive ambulances. In answer to your question how many people were killed by NATO, by mistake, collateral damage, I would estimate that it would be in -- maybe in the low hundreds, and every single one of those lives lost is a tragedy. My understanding is it doesn't compare with the thousands killed by Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll agree with the first part of your assessment, not the latter, though. Therefore, I will pursue this line of questioning. Do you know that in addition to the targets belonging to the Serb police and military, NATO also targeted some facilities holding members of the KLA or perhaps Albanian civilians specifically in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Istog prison. There was a prison which -- which they hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You were talking about the huts or cottages holding members of the KLA. You said so in the Milutinovic trial when you testified. You said it was your opinion that the incident was by no means a coincidence. You talked about that column of tractors, that convoy of tractors, on which civilians were travelling. You mentioned that, too, didn't you? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a -- sorry, we were talking at -- there is -- if you're talking about the incident where a column of tractors was bombed, yes, I reported about that, and I was concerned that it was a set-up job, essentially -- and this is what survivors of that incident told me, that they had been, if you like, they had been corralled into a place, held there by the Serb forces, and then NATO bombed it. And one reading of events is that the Serbs had become alerted to the fact that if they put military messages, military communications out of any place, then NATO would come along and bomb it. They would find the signals and put rockets into wherever the signals were coming from. Therefore, one reading of this -- what happened at that place with the tractors was the Serbs had deliberately blown up these people and then -- who were Kosovar Albanian and then showed it to the -- those journalists who were in Serbia as evidence of NATO's bloodiness, where in reality an entire different picture was potentially the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll agree with you to the extent --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean to interrupt my learned colleague, but I just want to ask if it was possible for him to indicate, each time there's a reference to the witness's previous testimony in the Milutinovic trial, to the statement, if we can have appropriate references, because so far none have been given when there have been references. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This has been raised yesterday, Mr. Djordjevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I agree with my learned friend. I entirely accept what she's suggesting. But if the witness were to answer that what I was suggesting to him was not true, then I would draw up the reference. But the witness answered in the affirmative, and that's why I believed it wasn't a good idea to waste any more time on that. Therefore, there is no need for me to call up the reference. That's at least what I believe, as long as the witness confirms what I'm put to him. May I continue my cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, that's not a satisfactory position, Mr. Djordjevic. If you're going to be referring to past testimony, especially from another trial but even previous testimony here, both counsel will need to be in a position to give a transcript reference so that it is possible for the other side to check. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, I entirely accept the suggestion of my learned friend. I stated my reasons, and I will try to comply in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were fully involved in what was going on in Kosovo, did you perhaps watch any coverage by ABC?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was in Kosovo, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In that case I will not have any questions to ask you about that. The Defence will be tendering that particular exhibit, but the audio was not particularly clear; therefore, I'm not moving to have it shown today until we get a proper audio-recording for that. My next question: During the wars in the former Yugoslavia, you suggested that you were in Vukovar, Osijek, Vinkovci, Zagreb, and Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question: While there, did you cover the war crimes committed by the forces of what was then Yugoslavia against the peoples living in those areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since you say that you covered those areas, were you also covering the areas during the operation performed by the Croatian forces known as Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one was Storm? When?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Operation Storm was the only operation marking the end of the clashes between the Croatian forces and the then still remaining Serbian people living in the Krajina area when Knin, Lika, and all the other areas were taken. There was a huge convoy containing many thousands of people that then left for Serbia. It was summertime. I don't think I can pinpoint the year for you. But what I want to know is, did you cover that particularly event? The event is generally known, and I want to use it as a reference later on.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe -- the answer is I didn't cover it because I wasn't -- my job had changed slightly, and I was not in former Yugoslavia in 1995 when I believe that -- when the Croat forces kicked the Serbs out of Krajina. So I wasn't there. But I was there in 1991, from 1991 onwards, and I saw horror on both sides committed by both sides. I was well aware of, for example, Serb -- Yugoslav People's Army, led and officered by the Serbs, shelling Osijek Hospital. It was shelled several times. But also at the same time there was innocent Serb civilians who had been shot at and tortured and killed by Croat fascists in -- or near-fascists inside Osijek, and I also reported on that, too. So although I missed Operation Storm because I was based in London, I was certainly aware of all the communities in Yugoslavia, and in particular I was aware of Serb aggression but also that many of the victims were Serbs and I understand that particularly true of the population in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the Serb aggression," what you mean is the attacks carried out by the JNA against the Croat-held positions, the Croatian people, Croatian targets, generally speaking? Is that what you were suggesting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you shell a hospital, that's aggression, and the Serb-led JNA shelled Osijek Hospital lots of times. They also shelled Sarajevo. I was also in Sarajevo in 1992. And at the time I didn't count them, but it certainly felt like it. People said they were shelling the city with 3.000 shells a day, and they shelled Sarajevo hospital, too, as well. So I use the phrase "Serbian aggression" advisedly and with intent. It's not necessary to shell hospitals. It's just plain wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you cover the crimes committed by the Mujahedin in Bosnia and the Al-Qaeda branch in that particular county as well as the vicious crimes they committed against Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't -- I would use the term Al-Qaeda with caution, and I would use the term Mujahedin with caution because I don't really think it applies. I've obviously heard the term because it was a big -- it was a big engine in Serb -- Bosnian Serb propaganda, in particular from Pale and the friends and relatives of Mr. Karadzic. However, I'm completely aware that as the war continued, all the communities - first, the Serb, the Croat, and then the Bosnian Muslims - became more -- there were more and more acts of barbarity and all three communities were -- had something to blame, none of them were innocent. I would say that as far as numbers are concerned, it was the considered view of fellow journalists like myself that the lion's share of violence had been committed by the Serb forces, and then in 1993 the Croats caught up killing people and the Bosnians -- the Bosnian Muslims were always somewhat behind. But yes, they did kill people and that, of course, is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was your coverage tantamount to what you're suggesting today from these various areas, the ones we're discussing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the word "tantamount" in this context. I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'll try to clarify. The backdrop to my question is this: Did you simply cover the crimes committed by the Serb forces, or did you also cover the crimes that were committed by the other sides in this conflict? And you suggested that there were crimes being committed by the other sides, and I have no trouble agreeing with you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. As a friend of mine called Paul Jenks who was killed in Osijek in January 1992. The official version of events according to the Croats and the government was that Jenks had been killed by a Serb sniper. I did a documentary for channel 4 and wrote several articles for The Observer suggesting that there was entirely different view, that in fact he had been killed by Croat neo-fascists led by a man called Eduardo Flores. So I am entirely open and have reported victim stories where the Serb forces may well have been innocent, and I have certainly reported on stories where Serbs have been victims. And I keep on returning to Osijek. It's partly because it's where I first saw the war in its full horror, but in particular remember doing a story, I believe that there were nine Serbs who had been killed in Osijek, who had been trapped, if you like, on the wrong side when the war started. And there was an old man and his son who were shot and dumped in the river. The son died; the only man managed to survive. I went to see him on the Serb side, and he told me a story which I found entirely credible, with him managing to escape. So it's absolutely true that I have covered all sides of it, and I'm also aware of the growing Islamicisation on the Bosnian Muslim side. To be fair, as I said, the lion's share of my reporting was from 1991 to 1994, and I didn't go back in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I thank you for this answer, Mr. Sweeney. Next question. Can you please clarify this: You said yesterday that channel 4 wanted you to tape massacres. I believe that was the phrasing used. What sort of massacres? Perpetrated by whom, by which side? You said, "They asked me to tape some coverage on massacres."

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, to answer your question -- actually, while we were talking, I was thinking in particular about the balance of my reporting. For example, I have reported on the massacre in Little Krusa. We also reported on the fact that the Albanians burnt down the Serb homes, and we showed it in our film, because I believe that to be objective and fair reporting. On the question of this -- of how I came to make these two films, I went to them because I met some of the men who had survived by running away from the -- from the selection, from the massacre that happened in late March, and these were -- I believe that these were men who lived on the western side of the river and their escape was more easy. They were the men who I met in very late March or very, very early April. I then went home to London for Easter and talked to channel 4, and channel 4 commissioned a film specifically about -- what was in my mind, what specifically was about the massacre in Mala Krusa, Little Krusa. But the idea that channel 4 would come to me and say tape a massacre, any massacre, they wouldn't do that. I wouldn't want them to do that, and that would be wrong. That didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, too. Now it's all much clearer. What I want to know is this: Did you ever learn that the KLA had committed any sort of crimes or abduction, anything like that, against Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You'd have to be blind and deaf not to realise that. For example, Belgrade TV constantly reported abductions, kidnappings, torture and murder, and killings by the KLA, and we were well aware of them, and they happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That was coverage on Serbian TV, which can be taken to be Serb propaganda, as simple as that. What I want to know is any personal interest you held in things like these going on.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I didn't come across anything like that in Little Krusa, but bear in mind that my focus from a very early age, or very, very early stage was on Little Krusa, and I didn't come across it. I was aware of it happening because I was aware of, you know, of the wider story. But nevertheless you've got -- you know, look at the population. In Kosovo I believe the population was nine-tenths Kosovar Albanian and one-tenth Serb. So you have a situation like apartheid, and I did go to South Africa during apartheid, the very, very end. And where you have a small minority trying to keep down a much, much bigger majority, you can only do that by fear and torture and killing. And so the lion's share of the killings was by the Serbs against the majority Albanian population, not the other way around. To ignore -- or, rather, to treat both equally would be unfair and wrong because it wouldn't be telling the whole truth. And the whole truth was that a minority of Serbs were repressing a majority of Albanians, and that eventually led to NATO's action and, by way of consequence, the attack by the Serb forces on the Albanian population. And I focused on Little Krusa. Had there been a story of abduction or torture by Dimitri Nikolic and his family, then we would have found out about it, and we would have reported about it, but there wasn't. Because when there was evidence of violence or wrong behaviour by the Albanians, for example, the burning of the -- of the Serb homes, we reported it. Just on the question of propaganda, the problem with Serb TV was that it never, ever appeared, it appeared to me, to question its own side. So there was a friend of mine who worked on the OSCE and he -- there was a story on -- it was reported that a family of five Albanians had died in a road accident. They were on a tractor. He described what happened in reality, as far as he told it. It happened in 1998. But the family were coming down on the tractor, and a team of MUP guys were ambushing them because they thought they were KLA arms smugglers. And they shredded this -- with so many bullets, they shredded this tractor and only afterwards realised that it was a family and there were no guns. And that was reported as a car accident, a traffic accident. So we had a real difficulty in trusting Belgrade TV's output. But on the wider question of Albania, just to give you, I think, some sense of doing stories that question what your own military does, I did a story later in 1999, which was well evidenced, with a Danish colleague which said that NATO had bombed the Chinese embassy in Belgrade deliberately. So, now, there's lots of evidence for that, and it's a very simple point, is that caused -- it was front-page news in The Observer, and it went all the way around the world. Now, the point about that story is that NATO, the Americans, and the British, hated the story, went around denying it, and it caused a major diplomatic embarrassment with the Chinese Government, but nevertheless we had the evidence to run it. The idea that I would in some way fabricate or exaggerate the story presented to me by these Albanian victims as some part of pro-NATO propaganda, that's -- I would resist that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite certain that I've now got an answer to my question, Mr. Sweeney. This was a comprehensive answer, and I had no intention of interrupting you. My next question, Mr. Sweeney: Where do you get the information that the operations performed by the Serb forces were planned? Where do you get the information that this was an act of ethnic cleansing? That's another thing you suggested. Where do you get any information on a chain of command from the top down and any actions that were planned along these lines? This is several questions, not a single one. I am sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nema problema. "Where do you get the information that the operations performed by the Serb forces were planned?" No one told me. It's by deduction, but it's simple. When Mr. Abduli and others said that after the NATO strike -- the NATO strike was 8.00 in the evening on the Thursday, if I'm right, and on the Friday told me there are 750 men in 15 buses, obviously requisitioned, arrive at Little Krusa, and there are tanks and armoured cars, half-tracks, and the Serb men are in police uniform with militia. That requires an enormous amount of planning, because Kosovo -- this part of Kosovo is right at the bottom. It's a long, long way from where those buses came from. So I believe that that required a lot of planning. Then you have the evidence of the cover-up. So the Albanian refugees told me that their friends and family and loved ones had been murdered. I got to -- the NATO invasion of Kosovo took place on the 12th of June. I went in that day. I believe I went to Little Krusa for the first time on the 17th of June, but we were still ahead of the Albanian refugees who didn't know whether it was safe to go back. When we arrived the hay barn was no more. It had been blown up. There were two holes in the ground. And that also requires organisation. There were no dead bodies, and we were looking for more than a hundred dead people. And moving all of those bodies and blowing up the barn, that also requires organisation. And I used to -- you know, I know what former Yugoslavia was like. You couldn't do that unless you had organisation from the top. How on earth do you get rid of a hundred dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, you said it yourself, and it's a generally known fact: There was a state of war that had been declared in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the reason being the air-strikes being carried out by NATO. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a certain point when I believe western governments became sick of the sight of Albanian Kosovar civilians being murdered, and they wanted it to stop. They asked Mr. Milosevic to stop it. He didn't and eventually the strikes happened. Then there was an immediate reaction, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. There's no need to dispute this. This would open other avenues and the discussion might become very broad. We're here to ask questions and provide answers. That's actually the only thing we're allowed to do; therefore, I'm not objecting to this last answer. Mr. Sweeney, when my learned friend Ms. Kravetz got your information, your details, from you, we also heard, unless I'm mistaken, that you completed the London School of Economics. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is the part of your statement true where you say that you did not go through any sort of military training? Your statement dated the 22nd of January, 2002; and the 23rd of January, 2002; and the 24th of January, 2001. More about this before you provide your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the Court's assistance. This is 65 ter statement D001-4054. That is the statement in English. Can a copy please be provided to the witness, and can the witness please have a look at page 2 of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I've got one already.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it perhaps necessary to have the statement on our screens for the benefit of the Chamber. Fine. Page 2 in that case. Thank you. We still have page 1. That's right, move on to page 2. Thank you. We have agreed to provide appropriate references from now on. I will now follow suit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, is it true what your statement claims: "I have no previous military training ..." That's how the paragraph begins.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. More about this, Mr. Sweeney. Did you perhaps complete any form of training allowing you to become an expert in military and police matters, political matters, historical background, even perhaps a forensic expert? Did you receive any sort of additional training in those fields, and I mean formal training?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You made certain statements about the political situation that prevailed in the country. You made these to the OTP in your capacity as a witness. I consider them to be worthless for this reason. I believe we have to drop these statements, and I'm not entitled to take them into account. A witness is only allowed to tell us what he knows and not what he believes or thinks. That portion of your statement is problematic and open to challenge. That's why I asked you this question. I will press on with my cross-examination until the break. I have a couple of questions left before the break. Mr. Sweeney --

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer the point that you've just made?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit snobbish. Just because you've not been trained to understand something formally doesn't mean that you're not allowed to report on it. I am a former British journalist of the year. I've helped free in Britain eight people accused of murder or manslaughter, thanks to miscarriages of justice starting with Sally Clark in 2001, and I have been to lots and lots and lots of war zones. And so when I see evidence of a cover-up of a massacre, I'm entitled to say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, no, by no means, that was not the purpose of my question. The purpose of my question was this: You provide opinions, you provide conclusions about the political, military, and police-related situation, the historical background, and the forensic aspect of this situation. Everything else you are saying, I have no objections and I believe you're perfectly within your rights. I do believe we have an understanding on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have page 5 displayed on the monitor, please and thank you, of Mr. Sweeney's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, can you please look at paragraph 4, focus on paragraph 4 -- 3.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We come here to something that I said I would be asking you about at a later stage. You obtained information from witnesses, that is what you call them, that the Batusha hangar was precisely where the bodies were now. Is that a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So we're clear, I'm looking at paragraph 3 on my screen. Is the paragraph that begins in English: "The hole was about 10 feet in diameter ..."? Yeah? To that extent, I'm not relying on witnesses. That's my own observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Sweeney, but I wish to clarify things completely. You say that the holes that you personally saw were most likely a result of a dynamite explosion. Since you had no military training prior to that, I wish to ask you: Do you know what consequences a dynamite explosion leaves or another type of explosive, such as TNT, not to enumerate all other explosive devices? And before you learned of this, did you contact any team? For example, you said that a team arrived later on from Great Britain. I believe they were from Scotland Yard and that they conducted investigation in various locations, including this one. Is this how you learned that this was a dynamite? Is this how you know that the holes that were there came as a result of a dynamite explosion, or is this an assumption on your part, and you don't have any reliable information about this, but this is what you think about it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: My cameraman who was with me is James Miller. He was killed in Gaza in 2003. But he, I believe, had -- I think he trained with the Irish Guards. He had, I believe, some military experience, and I think James thought exactly the same as I did. But it's right to say I've had no formal military training. It's also true to say that I was -- reported the wars of former Yugoslavia, and I reported the -- NATO's invasion or, rather, the British and American invasion of Afghanistan and the western invasion of northern Iraq in 1991 and again in Iraq in 2003. I've also been to war zones in places as different as Burundi and Angola and all sorts of civil unrest. So I'm not saying I'm a forensic expert. Far from it. On the other hand, I'm looking at a big hole in the ground and next door there is a hole in the building. It looks as though there has been some big explosions, two explosions in the Batusha hay barn. But I don't think you can say because I haven't had a formal training or I've never been in uniform I can't make that deduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any witnesses among Albanians who confirm to you that the Serb forces had come and blown up that hay barn with specifically dynamite, or was that another one of your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, obviously not, because all of the survivors of the hay barn massacre fled immediately they could. The -- and nobody was left around other than the Serb population, the Serb community, of the village. So the dynamiting and the cover-up and the removal of something like a hundred dead people, dead bodies, would have taken place, and there were no Albanian witnesses. So I don't -- as I said, it was a deduction. Was it dynamite? I don't know, but it was some explosive force. A hole in the ground -- two holes in the building next door. What cause could you ascribe to this other than some explosion? Am I missing something here?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me, although I'd rather not discuss this, it could have been an explosion of a gun grenade, a mortar grenade, an air bomb or some other thing. But this is why I asked you whether you had found any traces of this particular explosive or some other evidence, any piece of this hay barn that would led to this conclusion. That's why I asked you this question. I read carefully your report. I spoke -- I saw what you wrote about wheelchair and the soil particles and that's why I put this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes this part of my cross-examination, and I think it's time for a break. I don't think it would be a good idea to move on to a different set of questions in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll have the first break now and resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we now see page 9 of this witness's statement. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, now before you, you have page 9 of this transcript that we have referred to several times. Please look at paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before we go on to that, may I just go back to what you said earlier. I ascribed the holes in the ground in the Batusha hay barn to some kind of dynamite, and you said it could have been the explosion of a gun grenade, a mortar grenade, an air bomb. Now, I think you're wrong about that for the following reasons: A grenade or a mortar grenade would cause significantly small damage, almost like a grenade would cause a football, a mortar a bit more damage, but nothing like that size, and an air bomb -- a bomb from the air, I saw one in Chechnya, you have a big hole, but all of the hole is created, as you would imagine, from an object falling from above down. Now, had it been a bomb from a plane, you would have expected the next building to be flattened too as well. It wasn't. So that's why I believe the hay barn was in some way dynamited by an explosion. "Dynamite" is just a layman's term as far as I'm using it. But I'm going to stick with that, and I don't accept any of your alternatives. I just wanted to be clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Believe it or not, I truly do not have an opinion on that. There are experts that we will be able to consult. There is also a photograph that you took of the house and one can see the damage and the broken windows. This is much more significant damage than those holes that you're mentioning. Thank you for this additional explanation. Now, page 9, paragraph 5, you speak about evidence of organisation and the chain of command, and you say that it can be deduced based on the fact that these buses had licence plates from Nis, Leskovac, and so on, and these vehicles had come to Kosovo. You also mention a gentleman here, a gentleman from Subotica, and once again you came into contact with him through witnesses mentioned in your statement. However, what I have to ask you in relation to what you have said in your statement in paragraph 5 that is now before you is this: It is not clear to me based on what did you conclude that there was evidence of organisation and the chain of command and so on, given that these were legal activities of a country that was in war? What is so unusual about it? One knows that in wartime one uses all resources, that these are huge costs, especially for a country that was under sanctions at the time. There were no fuel, and so on. It was the civilians that suffered most of the time, not Milosevic and other leaders of the country. So what was so unusual, abnormal about it? Why do you conclude that this was a chain of command, organisation, and so on? In my view, these were quite normal activities. Would you agree with me or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is an enormously long question and getting longer. Could you limit it -- I think you've made your point quite clearly and the witness may be able to respond, but I don't think it's going to help us, and it's certainly taking a lot of time when you get these very long questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, just --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I accept your comments.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just one clarification. I see there on the transcript there is a gentleman from Subotica. I don't know if this was a problem with the interpretation of the question, but I don't see any reference to that in paragraph 5, so I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question was getting, I think, beyond the capacity of those trying to record it, it was getting so big. What we might do is hear the witness's reaction to what you said so far --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can I repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think you need to repeat yet. Let the witness react if he can, and then you may want to put something more specific following his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you made the point that these were quite normal activities. Well, forgive me, but the murder of a hundred -- more than a hundred men and boys in a hay barn is not a normal activity. That's a war crime. The organisation -- and I believe that it happened because I believe what the Albanians had told me, separately and together, but I believe they're not lying. They're not making it up. And therefore the question about organisation: Buses, 15 buses, an awful lot of men, buses from places far away from Kosovo. The blowing up of the hay barn, or certainly what we're looking at is evidence of something that I believe has been dynamited, and then the disappearance forever of more than a hundred men and boys. They've never come back. Now, they've been murdered and their bodies have been disappeared. That requires organisation, organisation of the militia men to come from Serbia proper, from the buses from Nis and Leskovac, for the men to be on the ground; organisation to select the men and boys away from the women and the children, as evidenced by the Albanian witnesses; organisation to place the men with their hands over their heads, the machine-gunner to be in place to kill them, and then to try and destroy the evidence. All of that requires organisation. We're talking about more than a hundred people being killed here. You can't do that in any normal, ordinary open democratic society, like we have in western Europe. You just can't do that. If the British Army did that in anywhere it was fighting in anywhere in the world, we would report it in seconds flat. You cannot kill a hundred people and get rid of their bodies without organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please don't tell me about the British Army. I would rather not get into that discussion. So it is your position, it is your claim, that those forces that had come in buses committed this crime.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The -- well, that seems very, very likely. I can't say for a fact who committed this crime. What I can do is set out the evidence that we've set out in the film. The Albanians say, the Albanian women and children say, there was a selection and there are multiple people who are ordinary farming folk - they're not sophisticated; they are not urban; I don't think they are conspirators; I believe that they were telling the truth. And they recognised some of their neighbours and they saw and they were terrified of the Serb forces which arrived. Then they hear the machine-gunning. There were six witnesses in the hay barn, men who survive because they're covered in blood; they're protected by their dead friends and brothers and sons. Now, the people who did this were Serb forces. That is what they say, and I believe them. There is more than enough corroborative evidence for the picture which they tell to be true. If there was some big gaping hole in this chain of evidence that they told me that we found, then I would report it because that's my job. And would never do something -- I wouldn't tell lies or put lies out. Now, there are some things I can be confident about and some things you hear are hearsay. It's absolutely true to say that I spoke to dozens of these people and their story together made absolute sense, it fitted, and it's a story of a massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We have heard about that yesterday. My question had to do with the organisation. It was clear and brief and you gave a very lengthy answer. And I will now move on. I don't want to dwell on this or put additional questions. Now, again, the same page of your statement, paragraph 7 this time. Would you please look at it. You say there that experience has shown that nothing happens in the former Yugoslavia without an order from the top. Would you agree with me that you said this in a negative context, with a negative connotation, given your experience from 1997 when Milosevic, as you say, sent tanks against students, including 1999 in relation to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, forgive me. I'm looking at page 7. I can't find the paragraph you're relating.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Page 9.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 9, paragraph 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At this time ..." yes. Yes, that's my statement and I agree with it. I agree with myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question had to do with this: Given your experience from 1991 until 1999, did you say this in a negative context, with a negative connotation, in relation to Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the constitution of the then-Yugoslavia, at least partially?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a great deal. As I say, I've studied a bit of politics, and one of the things that it struck me about was that a constitution of a country could be marvelous, and the reality for life in that country could be disastrous. So, for example, the constitution of the Soviet Union which I studied in 1977 to 1980 was glorious. The reality of life in the Soviet Russia was miserable. So I wouldn't have studied or looked at the Yugoslav constitution in any great detail for that reason. But also I'd add that my views on the constitution of Yugoslavia are, frankly, to my mind, are neither here nor there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the statement that you made, do you not find it strange that the leadership of a country has the right to make a decision as to whether a state of emergency would be introduced or not? On the 24th of March, middle-European time, that this country was attacked and was suffering continuous air-strikes for 74 hours. Does it strike you as strange that the top leaders of that country took that decision?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The story is much more complicated than that, but no, it doesn't strike me that they reacted in that way. It doesn't strike me as strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sweeney, for your very precise answer. Do you think that the incidents in Kosovo happened because orders had come from that -- to that effect from the very top? We're talking about Mala Krusa specifically. Do you have any evidence to back this up in terms of witnesses telling you about any links between the very top in Belgrade, the leaders, and those who were the immediate perpetrators on the ground, as it were?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You can deduce something -- I believe you can deduce something from the organisation on the ground. Separately, I did a story about something called Operation Horseshoe, which was a story that said that the leadership, the Milosevic leadership, had set out to ethnically cleanse Kosovo. But, again, this is a story like the numbers. This is a story that I was given but I -- or I sourced, but I didn't -- there is a different quality of evidence in that story and the eye-witness descriptions I've got from Mala Krusa and the evidence of my own eyes in Mala Krusa, which make me say to you that I will rely -- I will say that there was a massacre in Mala Krusa. I'm not so sure about, for example, Operation Horseshoe. Whether the story is true or in some way fabricated, I don't know. But that was -- certainly the Albanians and the people connected with the KLA leadership were saying it was part of a plan from the top, from Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, as far as I remember while I was preparing this cross-examination you stated at one point that the source for all your knowledge about the Horseshoe Operation was a source from the German intelligence agency, the BND; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be right in part but not -- I'm sure I would have checked it with somebody else, with other people as well, so I would have thought a number of sources, quite a few of them Albanian. It's never a good idea to base a story on one story -- on one source.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any Serb sources that you were using for that story?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had -- funnily enough, I did have a good friend who had been a former police officer in Belgrade, so I had some Serb sources, diplomats as well, but nothing -- nobody at the top of the Milosevic regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This Serb friend of yours, the policeman, did you ever put his name forward as a potential witness in this trial?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was answering a general question, I think, generally. This guy was not in Kosovo, doesn't know about the massacre in Mala Krusa. In terms of what he was good at was telling me what the mindsets of people in Belgrade was and particularly the mindset of the opposition to the Milosevic regime was and some, you know, juicy bits of gossip. But he didn't know anything about Mala Krusa or Kosovo in particular. I did because I ended up going there myself personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We spoke about the Horseshoe Operation, not about Mala Krusa, but your answer is still sufficient, since you said there was a lot of gossip circulating, stories, hearsay. My question is about the piece you say you wrote upon receiving word that the Serb forces would commit a crime against another ethnicity or some ethnic cleansing in Kosovo. When did you publish that? Which year? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's in my statement somewhere. May I have a look at it? Yeah, it's on page -- if you look at page 10, it says: "From March until November 1999 ..." I'm just reading from my statement now, "I was in Albania and Kosovo for extended periods of time. Early on I heard about Operation Horseshoe. This was a Yugoslav government plan to ethnically cleanse Kosovo by military action against the Albanian population" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down when he reads. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. [Previous translation continues] "... targeting the border areas first. Operation Horseshoe was allegedly first identified by the German intelligence agency, the BND, and picked up in Time Magazine." And I go on to say: "I have no firsthand knowledge of any documented planned operation." Reading that, it's clear that my source is Time Magazine, i.e., something in Time magazine, not German intelligence. So it's absolutely the case that my source -- my sources for this -- I believe I read this story and then checked it out with some Albanian Kosovar contacts, and I got hold of more information. And I wrote that story in The Observer I believe in early June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand, you say that you partially had a source from the BND and now you're saying the Times alone. But alright, this piece that was published in the Times, would you agree with me that it was published somewhere in mid-March 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may well be. I have a good memory but not so good that I can remember every single event or publication or thing I published from ten years ago. However, to be fair, once I found that paragraph in my statement, it's clear that what I said in my statement is correct, and what I said five minutes ago in this court was wrong. I didn't have a source in the German intelligence agency; I was relying on what I'd read in Time Magazine. And that triggered a line of inquiry which ended up in a story about Operation Horseshoe. But as I said, I bottomed it out by talking to other people. So I wouldn't just take somebody else's story and pass it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: Mr. Sweeney, did you write about Kosovo after the entry of NATO into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, basically I was in Kosovo for my paper, The Observer, so that I was writing -- which is a weekly paper, and I was writing a story pretty much every week because it was the biggest story in the world at the time. So I was writing stories from Albania about the massacre in Little Krusa as evidenced by the witnesses who had managed to survive and escape and the women and children. That was from the spring, from March onwards. Then I was waiting in Macedonia to go in on the heels of NATO, and then I started reporting on a series of stories from inside Kosovo. I was drawn by the -- what had happened in Mala Krusa because it struck me as being a shocking example of something that had -- well, it was a shocking story that I wanted to concentrate on and get to know it as well as possible, but I was also doing other stories at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, do you know what the KLA is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a -- the Kosovo Liberation Army, the UCK. Many people, many Serbs would say that it's a terrorist organisation that thrives on killing, murder, and abduction. Others, Albanians, in particular Kosovar, would see it as a liberation army. And my view would be somewhere in the middle of those two perspectives. It was both some kind of liberation army; also members of it, leaders of it, killed and abducted and tortured and did disgusting things for no proper good reason. Militarily it wasn't particularly competent and the sources in the British and American military were pretty dismissive of it, of its ability to do anything in serious terms, in terms of changing the military picture on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the fact that certain western countries declared the KLA to be a terrorist organisation? Do you have any information indicating that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Which ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. I can't be expected to answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, it's -- my question is -- you've asked me a question which assumes something to be a fact. I'm questioning the basis upon which you ask that question because I find it surprising, and so I'm interested to know the basis on which you say that a number of certain western countries declare the KLA to be a terrorist organisation. You may well be right. I'd just like to know which ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you about a country that was among the first to recognise Kosovo, the United States of America; however, this is no time and place for a discussion. I do have certain knowledge of that. I asked you about your knowledge, any knowledge that you had, and you said none. That is a very satisfactory answer in my perspective -- from my perspective. Mr. Sweeney, there is something else that I would like to hear from you. Do you know anything about any crimes committed by the KLA against Serbs and civilians at the time when the events at Mala Krusa took place? I'm talking about March and April 1999 and then all throughout this time up until the entry of NATO. That is what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, in relation to your previous point, in what context did the United States of America declare the KLA to be a terrorist organisation? Was it an expressed statement by the White House, was it the view of the State Department, or was it, in a sense, from -- where's it come from? What's the source? Because I'm -- I believe I've got a memory of this, so I'd like to know a little bit more about that point, because I don't remember, for example, President Clinton saying or behaving as if the KLA was a terrorist organisation in the same way that Hamas or the American -- the Bush administration considered Hamas to be a terrorist organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, I'm telling you again that I just want to know whether you had any knowledge about this or not. We can have a private talk once your evidence has been given here about all these various governments and what they said about this.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, you're presenting something as a fact to me, and I'm just hesitating and saying, Are you sure about that? I don't need to have a private conversation. But the point is this: If your question to me is am I aware that the KLA or people in the KLA did disgusting things to the Serb population, yes, I am, and we were very conscious of that. And there was -- there were a number of -- I remember, I believe, there were two brothers who were killed and abducted in, I think, 1998, and there were a series of terrorist outrages by the KLA on the Serb population. But their number and the number of dead Serbs was small in comparison to the number of dead Albanians in 1998, and in 1999 the numbers of dead Albanians grew and grew and grew, in particular after the NATO air-strikes, to a completely horrific degree. So it is not a question of comparing like with like. But if your question is: Did the KLA commit terrorist acts? The answer has to be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid you are again speaking about something that you have no specific information about, but since that seems to be a chosen mode, I really have nothing to counter that. Let me ask my next question. Following NATO's entry, do you know anything about any KLA crimes against Serb civilians, such as abduction, torture, kidnapping, murder? Are you aware of the horrifying story about the organs of captured Serbs being sold to third parties?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- sorry, you asked me two questions. Yes, obviously, I'm aware that Serb civilians were abducted and tortured and killed and murdered by members of the KLA. As I said, the lion's share of the violence was by the Serb forces against the Albanian population. I'm not aware of the story about the organs of captured Serbs being sold to third parties. I certainly didn't come across that in Little Krusa. And I'm a little bit skeptical, but no doubt you've got lots of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sweeney. My next question is about your arrival in Kosovo. I will allow for the possibility that you were mistaken about the 14th of June being the date you entered Kosovo, which is what you shared with us yesterday, on the front of a British tank. In your statement you claim the 12th of July, which I'm more inclined to take as the correct date, since this was a document that was produced shortly after --

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be fair, yesterday I said I wasn't clear about the dates.
