And this morning -- or rather when the session started today, I said -- I believe I said that I entered Kosovo on the 12th of July. And I think yesterday I said I wasn't sure whether it was the 12th or the 14th. But yes, you're absolutely right, it's the 12th of July -- 12th of June, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 12th of June, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the record, I believe it's -- it says in your question here, "In your statement you claim the 12th of July." Surely you mean the 12th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I said clearly the 12th of June. It was the interpreter who got the month wrong. So there's a correction there, and I think we both meant the right date.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question to you, sir: Who allowed you as a civilian to sit on a combat vehicle being used by the British Army? That is one thing that I'm slightly unclear about.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an enormous traffic jam. The British Army was at the head of it, and essentially there was a huge traffic jam of ethnic Albanians getting back into Kosovo to reclaim their homes, rebuild their lives. And the media, our car, was jammed up in the traffic jam, so I took my rucksack out of the back of the car, I walked to the front of the cue, and then I hitched a ride. I hitched three or four separate vehicles. I'm obviously British; I'm obviously English. I can talk immediately to the British Army and say, Can you give us a lift? And they did. It was the quickest way of getting to where I wanted to get to, which was Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The reason for my question is this: I know a lot about military rules, and I know that the British Army was in the middle of a combat operation at the time. Regardless of the fact that an agreement had been signed, the army's presence was necessary to protect and to intervene, to protect the civilians returning and to make sure there was peace in Kosovo. That was the official NATO explanation. I asked you about the permission you obtained. Was it informal or another kind?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another kind?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Any other way.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was informal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you armed on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would never carry a gun anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You say in your statement -- again, this is page 10, it's the statement that you have before you. That's what I believe. I haven't checked it. I think it's that statement. Two German journalists, your own fellow journalists, were killed and this caused you great concern. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who killed your fellow journalists?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The story we originally heard was that -- the gossip was, and remember this is -- this is a kind of war situation so it's very difficult to get hold of --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the truth. But we believe it was -- the story doing the rounds in Pristina was that it was Serbs who were opposed to Kosovo's -- sorry, NATO's intervention, who killed the two Germans. I don't know that as a fact. That was the story that was running around at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You have no other knowledge concerning this, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After this you rented a vehicle, and you were off to Mala Krusa, were you not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, you say you were the first to arrive in Mala Krusa, that it was deserted and one could still see the marks of Serbs leaving. Can we therefore conclude that the houses were all locked up? To begin with, and then I have a follow-up question?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were the -- James Miller and I were the first westerners to arrive there. I think that's absolutely right. There were still some villagers around, Mr. Shehu, a small boy who was in the film, are the two that stand out in my memory, but it was pretty much empty. The houses, the Serb houses by -- and there were some others. The Serb houses I think we didn't go into immediately because we were still kind of uncertain, and by the time we went into them, the doors had been opened -- for example, Sava Nikolic's house, somebody, presumably Albanian, had been in there beforehand and had kind of -- in a rough way had ransacked through the clothes and so forth, so they were lying around.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How long before you arrived could those Albanians have entered those houses, since you claim the doors were open?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe I arrived on the 17th of June in Little Krusa, and then we started filming. So it's entirely possible for Albanians to have gone into -- well, it was clear that somebody had gone into those Serb homes before we did. There was -- in one of the houses there was a sign saying, "Watch out for mines" in Albanian, so the Albanians had gone before. They hadn't destroyed and they hadn't burned the houses down. We were looking for photographs and videotapes, home videos, anything like that, which we could use in our television programme as evidence of you get faces. The Albanians, certainly the ones that lived in Little Krusa, didn't need to do that. They know exactly what these people looked like. So we were, in a sense, looking for different people. But I'm under no allusions. Some Albanians had been into those places before we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So it is your conviction that they looted the houses, taking away all the clothes, all the valuables, looking for money. I think you said something to the effect. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not my conviction; it's my guess, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you go into those Serb houses with some Albanians, or did you just go in with your cameraman?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have gone -- a lot of the time our -- we had two Albanian translators, first a woman and then a man, and he or she would have been with us. I believe -- I can't be -- he would have -- so there would have been myself and James Miller who would have gone into most of those houses and our Albanian translator, obviously not from Mala Krusa. I think we hired them in Prizren. But most of the time it would have just been me and James.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, are you aware of the fact that you had no right entering anyone's private property without special authorisation, or perhaps you can share with us today that you were in fact authorised in one way or another for that particular entry?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There had been a massacre of more than a hundred men and boys, the youngest of which was, what, 13 or 14. I was investigating that. That's why I was there. Now, I -- the idea that I would need special authorisation certainly -- doesn't that seem to be, in some way, slightly bureaucratic? What I'm trying to do is to put names to faces, maybe to secure evidence of who these people were. But that's the context I went in those homes, and I think that morally the context is entirely justifiable and to question it seems absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is possible, but that's just your position. Are you aware of the fact that you took possession of another's belongings in an unlawful way? And after all, Mr. Sweeney, this was far from being an honourable thing to do. You are no police officer; you're no investigator. You're a journalist, a citizen, a civilian.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll look at the record to see if it reflects what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question I heard, accompanied by quite a bit of comment, was: "Are you aware of the fact that you took possession of another's belongings in an unlawful way?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine. My answer to that is the same as before: I was investigating a massacre of more than a hundred men and boys. I had every reason to believe that this massacre happened, because I'd spoken at great length to the survivors of the massacre in Albania in April. We were now in June. So that I knew for a fact, as far as I was concerned, that these Albanian witnesses were telling me the truth, that their men had disappeared. I was now standing in the village. The Albanian homes were gutted and ruined, and there was a huge hole in the ground where the hay barn had been. In that light and in that context, I went and looked for evidence that would help me and the rest of the world, policemen included who weren't there at the time, to try and apprehend, at least identify the people who the Albanians said were responsible for this massacre. Now, that is a morally right and proper thing to do, and it is not dishonourable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, this is what I want to know: On that occasion you say you entered alone, for the most part, you and your cameraman. Did you have any evidence in relation to the persons you mentioned, any evidence identifying them as the immediate perpetrators of this unheard of crime in Mala Krusa, as you say? I mean Mr. Nikolic, Mr. Tasic, so on and so forth. Did a single Albanian tell you that they were the immediate perpetrators of the massacre at the hay barn?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, you've used a phrase there, "this unheard of massacre," "this unheard of crime." What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I mean the murder of 103 men in the hay barn belonging to the Batusha family. That is what we've been talking about throughout, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wouldn't characterize it -- use the phrase "the immediate perpetrators of this unheard of crime." I'm just puzzled by the use of the phrase "unheard of." So the answer so your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's stick to crime then.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good. Yes. As I said yesterday, the Albanian survivors and the women and children had identified these men. Now, as a result of the -- just doing some homework last night and this morning, I read through some of the articles that I'd written, and I can identify, I believe, when these various names came up. The first one is Mr. Dimitri Nikolic. Now, he used to, I believe, work in the local Rakia distillery along with Albanian colleagues, and he was well known to Granny Batusha. Granny Batusha is a vivid witness, and she said on tape, and it's in the first film and again in the second film, she said, I realised it was Dimitri. I saw him. Even though he had a microphone -- sorry, a camouflage balaclava on, she knew it was him and she shouted, Dimitri, and he turned his face away. And she actually acts like that. So I knew that I was looking for Dimitri Nikolic. Sava Nikolic, I believe, according to Xhelal Shehu had shot at them the first day, the Thursday before the massacre on the Friday, as they were running up into the woods on to the bluff. Sava Nikolic, I know the name, and I can't at this time remember who said, look out for Sava Nikolic, he was one of them. One of the survivors in the hay barn, I believe, saw Momcilo Nikolic. Those are the names. The key ones - Dimitri Nikolic, Sava Nikolic, and Sveta Tasic, those are the people I'm looking for. They lived in the village; their houses were looted but intact, and that's where I went to find evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As for your testimony yesterday, it is my understanding that you said that their Albanian neighbours recognised them, and that they were in police uniforms, all the persons that you mentioned, that is. However, as far as I can remember, I think that I seem to remember that you cannot say with certainty that they were the ones who opened fire. So could you please clarify that? You started talking about it today when you identified these persons as the persons who had been recognised; however, I asked you whether they were the perpetrators, whether these people directly said that the three of them were the perpetrators of this crime.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I'm going to be entirely consistent with what I said yesterday, and I'm saying that I cannot say for a fact -- listen, I wasn't there. I don't know. What I can say -- sorry, I do not know who ordered or commanded or organised the massacre, and frankly I don't believe it was these three or four names that the Albanians come up with, because I think that they were basically locals who were part of it. So that, yes, they are perpetrators because they were there. They could have done something to stop it, and they didn't. Yes, they are perpetrators. I don't think that they organised or commanded it, but they were part of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sweeney. My next question is whether you personally reported these persons to any prosecutor's office, court, or to the police? And do you know whether any criminal proceedings were instituted against these persons because of the war crime that had been committed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I told -- when -- The Hague investigators, the people from here, people from Scotland Yard, I told them the evidence I'd got, and I actually -- I believe the first contact was before June. But anyway, I told them and the Tribunal, or people working for the Tribunal, took this -- took the information I had and subsequently that led to the statement that you've got in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from that statement, are you aware of any other consequences of what you said to the Court, to the effect that proceedings were started against these persons in Serbia, in The Hague, or perhaps in a third country?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- if that's true, I'm -- I'd very much like to know about it. I am not aware of any proceedings against these persons in Serbia. Have there been any?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question: Since you mentioned the exact number of survivors, in your view, and also the exact number of casualties as a result of the incident in the hay barn in Mala Krusa, did you receive any information about the names of the persons who had been killed in the hay barn in Mala Krusa?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, going back to your earlier point, you asked me, Are you aware of any other consequences of what you said to the Court to the effect that the proceedings were [indiscernible] against these persons in Serbia. THE COURT REPORTER: Who? Sorry. I'm sorry, but can you start again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise, sorry. I'm just returning to that last point: Are you telling me that proceedings have started or have taken place against these people in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said to you. I asked you whether you had any knowledge of any proceedings taking place before any court, including this one here, against the persons that you referred to as the perpetrators and who were present on site? I'm talking about the Nikolic family, Dusan, Sveta Tasic, et cetera. That's what I asked you, whether you had any knowledge. I did not provide any information to you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I was mystified by the question. Right. Moving on, let me -- let me, I'm sorry, look at the screen so I can see what your last question was. I told the investigators from this Tribunal everything I knew and I gave them the evidence they wanted from me. That's what I did. I don't think that's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. My next question: Do you have any knowledge today about these persons? Are they all registered as missing, or perhaps do you have some information that is different?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it -- now, there is some concern or some doubt about the numbers, obviously because it's difficult. As I understand it, the last number that I heard was that 103 men and boys were killed in the hay barn. Six survived and then I believe that there were eight killed in the separate, smaller killing, which took place on the western side of the road in Mala Krusa, and in Velika Krusa, Greater Krusa, up the road, 20 dead. But let's just talk about Mala Krusa. The numbers, then, would appear to be well over a hundred dead in the hay barn, and I have heard nothing that challenges that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sweeney. In order to clarify the name of the river that you referred to, in all the records it says that it's the Drina river. For the record, could you please say what the name of the river is? Because that river is not called Drina. That is what the translation was, but I assume that you do know what the actual name of the river is.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If our translator said it was the Drina and they got it wrong, then I'm afraid I have just passed on that mistake. It's a river, and it's near Mala Krusa. I'm sorry if I've got the name wrong. I don't know the right name of the river. If you do, please tell me. I'd be always happy to be better informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, can we agree that the name of the river is Drim?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, can we? Because we've got three separate languages running around here. It could well be that what I've picked up is an Albanian translation or an Albanian phrasing of the river, not the Serb one. But the two aren't miles away, Drim or Drini. I defer to you. You're obviously right about the name of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that the Albanians call that river Drini, not Drina. But all right, Drina is a very well-known river and it's -- and it runs along the border between present-day Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Very well known. Let us move on to something different. You said that you saw a truck in the river. What is this that you actually saw? What kind of truck? Why did you mention that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because when I was up in the hills in March 1999, one of the witnesses, one of the men who first told me about the massacre in Mala Krusa, more than a hundred dead, and he was right about that, he said that he'd seen a lorry in the river and it was burning. And it struck me that the river was a good place to put burnt human remains. And let's remember, this mystery still remains. No one knows where these dead are buried. The people who lost these people, the mothers and the wives, don't know where -- where their dead are, and that is a continuing and unbearable pain for these people. It's awful to lose somebody and not know where their body is. So I was trying to find out. And we went, and we had a simple problem: The river was strong, and we couldn't risk losing the camera by taking it out in the middle of the river where we might damage the equipment, and it was a real difficulty. It's a difficult place, in particular at that time. So we couldn't get the shot that I wanted. But I went out there and swam in the river, and I saw what I thought looked like blood on the lorry. I'm completely aware of the possibility that your mind can suggest things that actually aren't there, so I may be wrong about that, and we don't have any precise evidence. I'm not forensic. By the time the forensic people came along, I think that the lorry had gone, moved down the river, or the moment was lost, or they didn't look. Nevertheless, where are the dead?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you indicate to any one of these pathologists at the time that you saw that truck? And if so, who did you speak to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're misunderstanding the scene. When we first arrived in mid-June, there were no pathologists. They only turned up much later, I believe in -- in -- in July, so three weeks later. So at the time there was only us, and that's why I tried to gather as much information as possible and as much evidence as possible. So I believe I did tell them about it, but it's up to them. What we did do was go and have a look, and we tried to film it, and we couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as we near the moment of the end of this cross-examination, I would be interested in hearing the following: Mr. Sweeney, did you investigate the broader context of the events in Mala Krusa?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Within that framework, did you have any knowledge about the activities of the Kosovo Liberation Army in that territory at the critical time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard stories. What the villagers told me, the Albanians, was that it had been very, very quiet there, and there had been a -- they were on good terms with their Serb neighbours, which is why the resulting -- what happened was so shocking to them. I believe it's entirely possible that the KLA used the -- kept trouble away from this area, the whole area, because it was a good place to run guns out of Albania into Kosovo. And if there was violence in, for example, somewhere like Mala Krusa, then that would have caused the MUP to come down, the police to come down, and then it would make the smuggling of guns more difficult. We had no direct evidence of this, and there was -- when we first arrived, there was no sort of KLA leadership of any kind there. The place was empty. So it was something that we were aware of. That doesn't excuse for a second the killing of all of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is not what I wanted to say, that that was an excuse for any single person to lose his or her life. My last question for you today,

utterances.speaker: MR. SWEENEY
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about killed or abducted citizens of Serb ethnicity from that area at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there was a -- there was a story in a village nearby that some Serbs had been abducted and I think killed. There was -- it was while we were there, but it was not in the village. It was not in Mala Krusa; it was some kilometres away in a zone organised by a Dutch battalion. We focused on Mala Krusa to the extent that, for example, I believe we mention it, but we didn't go in any detail into the smaller massacre in Velika Krusa of 20 dead. So because our focus was precisely on the chain of events and the massacre, that's what we stuck to. But you're absolutely right, there were Serb victims, and they were killed -- innocent Serbs were killed and abducted and tortured by the Albanians and the KLA, and that's wrong, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will agree with you, Mr. Sweeney. I feel sorry for the innocent Albanians and innocent Serbs and any innocent person who lost his or her life anywhere. At the end of my cross-examination, I'm going to thank you for the answers that you've provided, and that is how I'm going to end my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. Ms. Kravetz, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just -- sir ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would it help? There's a couple of dates of the films which you asked me about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, if you want to provide the dates, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you clarify the dates when your first documentary was broadcasted?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was broadcast on the 20th of 5th, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And your second documentary, "Prime Suspects"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN PAUL SWEENEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th of November, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure pleased to know that that completes the questioning in respect to this matter. Can we indicate our appreciation of your attendance here and the assistance you've been able to give. And we will arrange now, of course, for you to leave the courtroom, and you may go about your ordinary activities. Thank you, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness is Mr. Mehmet Krasniqi, or Avdyli. He also goes by that name. This witness will be led by Mr. Stamp who is on his way to the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm just looking at the time now, and I wonder whether it would be more practical to have the next break now and then resume with the witness afresh.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That would be convenient for us. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will give Mr. Stamp time to get here as well. I think we will do that, and we will resume, then, at 5.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. May it please you, the next witness is Mr. Krasniqi, Mehmet Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that's given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Stamp has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Could you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I am Mehmet Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: 19th of May, 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Has your surname, that is, your last name, always been Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: For some time I used the surname Avdyli.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when did you change to Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When in 1999? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I think it was September, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where are you from, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Krusa e Vogel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that place is sometimes referred to by the Serbian name Mala Krusa.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, Mala Krusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, prior to 1999 or prior to the NATO intervention in 1999, what was the -- about how many houses made up that village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There was a total of a hundred households, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic distribution like? About how many households were Albanian and how many households were others?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Seventy-three households were Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the remainder were?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Serbian, and three Roma households.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, prior to March 1999, how did the different ethnicities co-exist within your community, as far as you are concerned, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We didn't have any problems. We never had any problems with them. We had good relations. No trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I bring up the exhibit with the 65 ter number 00615. That is the booklet with maps of various areas. I just want to look at it briefly, just to get us oriented. And I'd like to go straight to page 22 of that booklet. We could probably zoom in a little bit more to the bottom of the page so that we can see all of the major towns. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the page here you see the main towns near to your village. You see to the top left the town of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To the right, Orahovac or Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Rahovec and Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And Prizren to the south, that's to the bottom right. Do you see where Mala Krusa is on this map? Can you make it out?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you circle Mala Krusa.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We see that's just on the border of Prizren and Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I just indicate that the witness has drawn a circle that really looks like the number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see other villages nearby, like Celine, Nogavac?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Zrze?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Xerxe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you just put a little tick beside these villages.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: So Xerxe, Celina and Nagavc. You want me to circle them?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Celine, Nogavac, and Zrze.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Nagavc, Celina and Xerxe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you also see Velika Krusa?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Also put some marks for Zrze, Celine and Nogavac. So you could just put a dot beside that as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I already did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we give this an exhibit number. I just have him mark his town and his village and surrounding villages because many of these surrounding villages are the subject of witness statements that have applied for 92 bis in respect to. So I just do this for the benefit of the Court, to identify the area, and you will see from his evidence later on that the -- some of these villages become relevant to the testimony. So I'd ask that the marked map now be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P301, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, on the 24th of March, 1999, the NATO intervention into Serbia, the former Yugoslavia, and Kosovo in particular, commenced. The next day, the 25th of March, did anything happen in your village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the 25th of March, the Serb forces came and surrounded the village, from the main road Prizren-Gjakove, and the population was concerned so they went up to the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. When you say "the Serb forces came and surrounded the village," what forces were these? Can you describe them a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Well, the forces of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did they have vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. They did have heavy artillery, tanks, APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And about what time did you observe that they were in the vicinity of your town or village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I saw them early in the morning. We could see the lights of the vehicles and the military machinery around the village. They stopped at the junction from the road Prizren-Gjakove and turned towards the village. It was before dawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximate time?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was about 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, when you observed these Serb forces, did you and your family do anything?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The whole people from the village were going towards the mountain. So I took my family, we left our house, and we went to the mountains as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Firstly, could you tell us about your family? What -- how many members of your family were there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: At that time there were four of us in my family - myself, my wife, and two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How old were the two children?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: My children were -- one of them, the son, was 2 years old; my daughter was nine months old.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I think you said in your -- in an earlier answer that -- the whole people from the village. Did the Serbs go into the forest as well?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, the Serbs did not leave to the mountains. They did not leave their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I'd like to bring on screen document 00099, and page 2 thereof. This is an aerial photograph of the village taken in 1999 by an ICTY investigator. Does this -- is this page 2? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is this the village -- is this your village, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you see your house on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you to put a letter 1 on your house -- not a letter, a number 1 on your house.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I put number 1 over my house, on the roof there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And does this photograph include the forest that yourself and your neighbours went to?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. But can you use an arrow to point to the direction of where the forest is? Mark an arrow, an arrow in the area where the forest is, pointing to where the forest is. Mr. Krasniqi, if you hold the pen ...

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Here. If you start here from the houses, this is the stream and the woods are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I can't see what you're pointing to. Just put an arrow that points us to the direction of the forest. That's what I'm asking you to do.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: My hand is trembling.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I think we understand what you're showing us. While you were in the forest did you observe anything happening in respect to the village that you had just left?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I couldn't see anything, but I could hear the noises from the main road towards the village, and I could see smoke coming out of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did the forces that had entered and surrounded your village do anything while you were in the forest?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We couldn't see what they were doing in the village itself. We were in the woods, close to the stream. But we could hear the shots, the gun-shots, and we could see the smoke coming out of the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Now, in the forest where you were towards the mountains, did anything happen in that area?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the 25th nothing happened. Only the gun-shots, and we could see the branches of the trees falling down because of the bullets. The branches fell on the ground, but nothing apart from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Bullets were being fired where?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The bullets came towards the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And from where?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: From the lower part and from the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, how long did you, your family, and the other villagers remain in the forest?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We remained there for the whole day, until the next morning. Some of them who had small children went to Sejdi Batusha's house, while the rest of us remained in the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who is Sejdi Batusha?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: He's a villager, a co-villager.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see his house here?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to take the pen, hold it carefully, and just put a 2 where his house is, on top of his house.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Those of you who remained in the forest, did anything happen to you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the 26th of March, when the police and the Serb forces ordered everybody to come together and go to Sejdi Batusha's house - the women, the elderly, the children. There were two disabled people; they couldn't walk. And they ordered for these people -- these two people to be brought where the others were as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They called their names from the window, Aziz Shehu and Sulejman Batusha were called to go and fetch those two disabled people and bring them to Sejdi Batusha's courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You're going a little bit ahead of me now. I'm still in the forest. Did any of the police come to the forest while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the 26th of March, the tanks climbed up the village and surrounded the village from the forest part, and no policeman came to where we were in the forest. But they told these two people to come and tell all the persons who were there in the forest to come to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you remember where in the village you went to?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: To Sejdi Batusha's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived there, did you enter the house, or did you remain outside?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We were all together - women, children, men. We were gathered together in Sejdi Batusha's courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what happened while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: When we were in the courtyard, we were told to go out to the street and they separated us, the men from the women. They told the women to go towards Albania or to get themselves drowned in the river Drin, while the men were told to create three rows and put their hands above their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. What about the little children, the very young children?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The women and children were told to go and drown in the Drin river or go to Albania, while children, boys 13 years of age and above, and all the men, including Bali Avdyli, who was 72 years old, were told to stay in the street and were told to put their hands above their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So what did the women and the young children do? Did they remain, or did they have to leave?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They went downwards, because the police gave the order so they started moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like you to put a number 3 on the map to depict the area on the road where the women and children were separated from the men. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you describe to us carefully who you saw there present ordering the men to line up in columns of three and ordering the women to leave, to drown themselves or to go to Albania? Who was doing it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There were several policemen with white -- with yellow and white ribbons on their arms, upper arms, on the street. They ordered us to produce our wallets and documents and give those things to them. And they were insulting us and asking questions such as, Where is NATO? Why is NATO not rescuing you? NATO will come and rescue you, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These people, these policemen, what colour uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They were wearing blue uniforms, dark blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, before that day, had you seen policemen in uniform like this before?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. We could see them in the village. They would come to Dimitrije Nikolic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, after the police separated you men from the women and children, did they order you to do anything or to go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They told us to get up with our hands up, not to look on any of the sides, just to look down. And they took us to Rasim Batusha's house, where there was this house with two rooms and a corridor. Rasim Batusha used to keep the hay for his animals there. They told us to get in the house. The corridor was full, and the room where I was, the other room as well. In the room where I was, there was fodder for the animals. And then they executed us, they shot at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see Rasim Batusha's house on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The place of the massacre? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Can you put a circle around that place, please.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, about how many men were forced into that house, or the house that was at that place?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There were 109 men forced into the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it a one-storey house or a two-storey house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Single-storeyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did it have windows or not?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: One of the rooms had just one window, while the other had two windows; one towards the street and the other opposite the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, about how big were these rooms of this house, in square metres, if you can?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Sixteen square metres, one of the rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was that the room that you were in?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, the room I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you know a villager by the name of Sait Hajdari?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. He is a relative, an in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know where he was?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: He was there among the men, together with the rest of us. When we were forced into the house, Sait Hajdari was in a wheelchair and he was left near the door, because it was impossible to put him further in. So they blocked the door with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, while you were inside this house that was used as a barn, as you described, could you tell us slowly what happened to you and the men who were in that house.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: A little while later when we were inside, they started shooting at us. The execution began, and there were people who were killed immediately. Others were not killed, and they were screaming and some were saying, "Please don't scream. Maybe they won't come and execute us one by one. Please don't scream." So some of the people were screaming. Shefqet Shehu looked outside the window because he thought that they had left. At that time he saw Momcilo Nikolic at the window. He was his neighbour. And he said, Momcilo Nikolic, are you doing this to us? And he's a Serb from our village. Momcilo Nikolic shot him -- shot Shefqet there and then and started to shoot at the bodies of the people as well. After that they put some liquid, incendiary liquid, in the room. I had Asllani close to me, an elderly person. His arm was hit by the bullets and he said, "My arm is cut off." So when they put that liquid inside, Zenun Hajdari was above me. He covered me in blood. My face, my jacket, everything I had on was soaked in blood. A little later they began to bring maize stems and put them on the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just if I can stop you there. When you said that they used a liquid, tell us more about that. What did they use the liquid to do?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They wanted to burn the people. Some of it, some of the fuel fell on my ear. I tried to wipe it away. For a month and a half my ear was -- I couldn't hear, and my face and my hands, which were burnt, got better sooner than the ear did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. So they started a fire in the house after the shooting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you actually see -- did you see the persons who were shooting into the house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know where they shot from?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: From the windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what type of weapons they used to fire into the house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know -- I don't know the names, but there was a box they had put down at the window that was linked to the machine-gun. They had put the machine-gun on that box.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see a machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: At the window, in the room where I was at the window. The barrel of the gun was inside the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you're telling us now what happened to you inside the house. How long did you remain in the house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I remained under the bodies for some time, until the blood I was soaked in dried. When they threw the maize stems on the bodies, I could no longer breathe because of the smoke. I started to choke. So that's when I stood up and said to myself, I'd better go out and die of a bullet than of fire. So as I got up, my face was caught in the fire and my hands, too, because I had to use my hands to get myself out of the bodies. So I left through the windows and went straight to my uncle's house, to the cellar of his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's see if you can identify on this map where your uncle's house is. Can you see it on this map that's before you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In relation to the circle that you put depicting the area where the execution took place, where is your uncle's house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It is adjacent --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Don't mark it yet. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It is next to the place of the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Just so we know exactly where you're talking about, just put a number 4 carefully on top of your uncle's house that you escaped to.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how long did you remain in your uncle's cellar?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Until it got dark, and that is when I left for the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, were you alone in your uncle's house, or were there other people there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was alone in the cellar of my uncle's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were in your uncle's house, did you observe the Serb police, who were in the village, doing anything?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I saw them enter the courtyard of my uncle's house. Three policemen took away the Mercedes car and a Renault 18 make. They started the car, and they let it drive into the wall on its own. Nobody was driving it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you saw this, where were you in your uncle's house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you escaped and ran to the cellar, and I take it from your answer that at some point you went to the second floor of the house.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you went to the second floor of the house, was it still day or was it night by then?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The persons who took your uncle's vehicle, the Mercedes, did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Only Sveta Tasic I knew, not the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, how well did you know him? Did you know him before?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: He was a Serb from my village. I knew him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you see anybody doing anything in respect to the house that was -- or the house where the execution took place? Maybe you don't follow what I'm asking. While you were on the second floor of your uncle's house, did you notice anything happening at the place where the shooting took place?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Probably it's because I'm --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They continued to bring in maize stems, two young men, and to throw them on the bodies, during the day. And policeman around the house, he was in company of young men, and he was saying, "If you see anyone move, don't feel sorry for him. Kill everyone you see."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When they were throwing these maize stems in the house, was the house still burning at that time, or the area where you were, still burning?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, can you recall about what time you left your uncle's house and went to the forest?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: At around 6.00 in the evening. It was dark. I left the house and went to the mountains. There, I saw two men running away. One of them was Refki Rashkaj and the other was Adnan Shehu. I was there in the mountains. I could see the house set on fire. They were still carrying maize stems and throwing them on the bodies. I could observe this from the mountains. I could see the house on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did anything happen to the other houses in the village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They were all burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did anything happen to the Serb houses in the village while you were in the forest?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, nothing was happening to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the forest?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I remained in the forest until Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many days would that be?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That would be Saturday, Sunday, and Monday, three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where did you go to after that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On Monday, before dawn, I went to Nagavc village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While there, did you receive any medical attention for your burns?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: When I arrived in Nagavc village, there were many people there. I first came across Ali Hoti, the doctor. He didn't have anything with him to treat my wounds. He said, Xhemajl Danaj is here. He might help. I went to him. He didn't have any material, so he used baby nappies to treat and dress my wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Xhemajl Danaj, he's a doctor as well?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, he's a doctor, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Nagavc village, you said there were many people in the village. What were these many people doing there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: People from Celina, from Krusa e Madhe, Hoxha [phoen] and Brestovc were there in Nagavc.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What were they doing there? Why were they there? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was not there, but they had been told to remain there, not to move about. People talked and told me that the Serbs had collected the money and the valuables from them and had told them to remain there in the village until they're further told to go to Albania. This is what I heard from the people on that day when I was in Nagavc.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of these people who were in Nagavc?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They were all Albanians and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did they eventually go to Albania?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. When Nagavc was bombed on the 2nd of April, at 2.15, we set off. We gathered first on the road, and from there we set off for Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which border did you cross through to go to Albania?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Qafe Morina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did anything happen to you while you were at the border?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. While I was crossing the border, they noticed that my face and my hands were burned. And they insulted me, they cursed me. They said, "You've been hurt by a shell. You're a soldier. Who is your commander? Where were you hit by this shell?" So they took me inside and tied me to a radiator.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who did this to you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The Serb forces, policemen. They were wearing police clothes, but there were also people from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the room they took you to, was this at the border post?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And how long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Until it got dark. I don't know the time, the exact time, but it still wasn't dark. Until dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you left to where?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They told me to go to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Before we get to Albania, the other people who were crossing into Albania from Kosovo at that border crossing, how were they treated by the border police?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They plundered them. They took their money, their identification documents. They were told to throw the documents in one spot. So when they noticed my wounds, they sent me back. All the people who were crossing the border, they were cursing them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where in Albania did you go to?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In the Berat area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you receive further medical treatment there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In Kukes I remained for three days. I was given medical assistance there, issued some medicaments. But I didn't want to stay in Kukes. I wanted to find my family as soon as possible. I didn't know anything about them, didn't know whether they were alive or dead. So I wanted to leave and refused to stay in the hospital. So I treated my wounds with bear fat, with alternative medicine. So this is how I lost all the scars, and I have no scars left on my face or my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I propose to show the witness a -- yes, I was going to ask permission to show a video, but I realise I need to tender this first. In the circumstances, I think I should return to it to have him do one more marking before I tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, while you were outside your cousin's house at the place where you marked 3 on this map, where the women were separated from the men, and during the time, that time to when you're taken to the house or the barn where the execution took place, did you see anybody, any member of the police that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: From there we were taken to the execution place. I could recognise two persons during this time - Dimitrije Nikolic, Zvezdan Nikolic, Momcilo Nikolic, Sava Nikolic. So these three were coming from the lower part. This is where I saw them and these were the ones that I recognised. The others ones I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you gave us four names there.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I made a mistake with Momcilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. So you didn't see Momcilo there.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who were these three persons - Sava, Zvezdan, and Dimitrije Nikolic? Did you know them before?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I saw them at the location where we turned towards Rasim Batusha's house, there at the junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, do you see that place on the photograph in front of you, the place where you saw them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you put a number 5 at the place where you saw these three persons.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They were dressed in police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did they or did they not have any weapons or arms with them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With what?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They were wearing their weapons on their soldiers. They're called Kalashnikovs, or I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see them doing anything in that place where they were?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: But they were coming towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, from the place where they were, could they have seen the house or the barn where the execution took place?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. The place is visible from where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I probably asked this before, but can you tell me, about how long did you know these people before?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We were born and lived in the village, all of us, so I knew them since I was a child, from birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said Dimitrije -- you used to see police in uniform going to Dimitrije's house. Did he operate a business of any sort at his house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We didn't know what kind of business he had. It resembled a sort of cafe. The Serb police would go there. The policemen would come by car and get drunk there. The children were scared to go to school by that road and the adults would avoid using that road, too. They would go out only if they had to go to the doctor or for other bare necessities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. While we are back at this place, can you tell me about what time it is you entered the house where the execution took place? About what time in the day, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't have a watch, but I said that it was approximately 11.00, 11.30. But I don't know the exact time; I didn't have a watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that's in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And about what time did you escape through the window?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That I don't know. I stayed for quite some time under the bodies, but I don't know for how long exactly. You could no longer hear any noise from the people. And when they threw this liquid and when the smoke came out, I started to choke. I touched the blood on my face and on my body, and it was nearly dried. So I could no longer breathe in there and that's when I said to myself, I will go out, and it's better that I get killed by bullet than be burnt alive. So I don't know what time it was exactly, but this is how I left and God saved me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you give us an estimate, a ballpark estimate, as to the time when you left?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: What can I say? I didn't have a watch. I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Your Honours, could this marked photograph be received in evidence and given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P302, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, do you remember approximately how many men and boys were taken into that house where the execution occurred?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't count them at the time, and I didn't do it now either, because it brings me pain. I don't know how many men and young boys were there, but all of us were taken into this room and from all that number, only six survived. But there were people starting from the age of 13. The youngest was 13 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were in Albania, do you recall giving a statement to people, to investigators from this Tribunal in regard to what happened to you at the barn or the house where the executions took place?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. I've given statements to all of them who told me they were from the Tribunal, but I don't know the dates when I gave these statements. I didn't take any notes of the dates, but I was at their disposal whenever they wanted to ask me questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In -- well, you just said that you don't remember how many people were taken to the room. Do you recall giving a statement on the 4th of April, 1999, when you compiled for the OTP Prosecutors a list of the names of the persons that you recalled then who were taken into the barn?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I remember giving a statement to the Tribunal and testifying. I don't know the date; however, I know that I did give them a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I propose to show the witness a statement just to refresh his memory, because he says he doesn't remember the number and the names of everybody that was taken to the barn. It is a statement of the 4th of April, 1999, and I don't propose to introduce it for the general -- the statements he makes in it about what happened to him. He has already testified to that. But just to remind him of the number and the names he compiled. It is 02341.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness may be shown the statement and asked if it refreshes his memory about those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think we need to go to page 7 of this document. Your Honours, I'm wondering if perhaps we could take this up tomorrow. I have left my copy -- it's a pretty long exhibit, and I have left my copy with the number -- the page numbers for the Albanian version, which is what I'd want to show him, while we look at the English version. And it probably would take some time for me to scroll through the document here to find the right page numbers. So I see it's just a minute before the normal adjournment time. Perhaps it would be better if we resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now, and we resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. Mr. Krasniqi, we have to finish for the night now, and we will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00, in the morning, 9.00. The court staff will give you further advice and assist you to be here in the morning. Thank you very much.
